title: Victory over death
hook: some early Christian writers saw the cross as Christ defeating death and evil

segments.voice: Yesterday, one person, two natures: fully God and fully human, held together without blending. Your line was both, not either. Where did you hold two things at once? Day one thousand eighty-two.

A gate lies flat on the ground, broken in two, its bolts scattered like dropped keys. A figure in white stands on the pieces. He's reaching down into the dark and pulling an old man and an old woman up out of their graves by the wrists. That's the Anastasis, the resurrection icon of the Eastern churches. Other Easter icons show the women at the empty tomb. This one shows a rescue, the moment the prison of the dead is smashed open, and Adam and Eve, the man and woman from the garden, are hauled out. For the next stretch of days, the question is a big one: what did the cross actually do? Christians give more than one answer, and some hold several together. Today's answer is a battle, and a winner.
screen: `ADAM AND EVE PULLED BY THE WRISTS.`

segments.voice: The Latin name is Christus Victor: Christ the victor. In this picture, humanity is held hostage. Death, sin and the devil have us, and nobody can break out from the inside. So God comes in. The Letter to the Hebrews says Christ shared our flesh and blood "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil." And it adds why that matters: to set free those who "through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage." Read that again slowly. The enemy isn't only death. It's the fear of death, leaning on a whole life. Paul's letter to the Colossians uses the picture of a Roman triumph, a victory parade: Christ "having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it." The powers that seemed to win on Good Friday are the ones paraded as the beaten side. Some early Christian writers told it almost like a trick. Death swallowed Jesus the way it swallows everyone, and found it had swallowed life itself, and couldn't keep it down. Gregory of Nyssa even pictured a fishhook hidden in bait. And then Paul, near the end of his first letter to Corinth, gets to taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" You can hear it at Easter in the Orthodox hymn that sings of Christ trampling down death by death. Churches can hold this picture alongside others, and over the coming days we'll meet several. This one says something simple: the cross was a fight, and the fight is over.

Here's the practice: name one thing that's lost its grip. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that has held you hostage: a fear, a habit, a grief, a voice in your head that says you're finished. Give it a plain name. Then picture it as the broken gate in that icon, lying on the ground. If you pray, you can name it to Christ as one thing he has defeated. If you don't, simply notice what it would feel like for that thing to have no last word. Breathe out slowly. The bell holds the time.
Christus Victor. Latin for Christ the victor: the cross and the empty tomb as a battle won over death, sin and evil.
Your line: death is defeated. When a fear leans on you today, say the old taunt under your breath: where is thy sting? Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: In Orthodox churches the Easter hymn proclaiming Christ trampling down death by death is sung again and again through the Easter season, and the resurrection icon shows Christ raising Adam and Eve from the broken gates of death; Protestant and Catholic Christians also sing and preach this victory, especially at Easter.

fork.setup: you're painting the Anastasis, the resurrection icon. which moment does it show?
options: an empty tomb with folded cloths.
Christ standing on broken gates, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their graves.

fork.reveal: the Anastasis paints the rescue: death's prison smashed and the first humans hauled out. victory, not just absence.

original.note: Greek: victory, the word behind "O grave, where is thy victory?"

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross was only a defeat that Easter reversed.
what it means: in this picture the cross is the battle itself. death swallows Christ and can't hold him, and its power is broken.
what a scholar hears: Christus Victor, Christ the victor. Hebrews names the real chain: the fear of death, holding people all their lives.

notes: The index hook says 'many early fathers'; per the claims rule the script says 'some early Christian writers' instead. Consider the index wording.
Fishhook image attributed only as 'tradition says one writer'; it is usually traced to Gregory of Nyssa (Great Catechism 24) and also appears in Rufinus and Gregory the Great. Confirm before naming.
Description of the Anastasis icon (Christ on broken gates, raising Adam and Eve by the wrists) is a common form; some versions differ in detail. Confirm.
Colossians 2:15 read as a Roman triumph image: standard reading, but interpretive.
The phrase 'Christus Victor' as a label is modern (Aulén); the script avoids dating it and does not claim the fathers used the phrase. Confirm the framing 'the Latin name is'.
Editor pass: cut 'the oldest-sounding one' and 'they often hold several together' (unsourced claims) for 'some hold several together'; 'every Easter' softened to 'at Easter'.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the hook, myth and fork had said the Eastern Easter icon 'doesn't show an empty tomb'; Orthodox Easter also uses the icon of the myrrh-bearing women at the empty tomb, so the icon is now named (the Anastasis) and the claim narrowed to it. Fishhook image now credited to Gregory of Nyssa (Great Catechism 24, already in sources) instead of 'tradition says one writer'. 'Led away in chains' overstated Colossians 2:15; now 'paraded as the beaten side'.
